unit-0.title: Unit 0: Welcome, Your Situation and Your Map
unit-0.deliverable: Learner profile, credit plan and map decision
unit-0.page:
This first unit is about you, so the rest of the course fits your school. The tutor will ask what orienteering you've done (or something like it, such as hiking with a map, geocaching or map games) and whether you've taught it, what your school and students are like, which spaces you can use and when, what you hope orienteering will do for your students, and what worries you about it. Doubts are useful to us. They show us where the course needs to do more.

Then three practical things:

- **Your map.** If you'd like an orienteering map of your school grounds or a nearby park, apply to Orienteering USA's Youth Mapping Program (YMP) this week. A mapper makes the map, which takes several weeks or longer, so it's worth starting now. Meanwhile you can teach the kit activities, which don't need a map. If you're applying, the tutor walks you through the application (add about 15 minutes); see below.
- **PD credit.** Navigation Games isn't a registered PD provider yet, so find out who approves professional development hours for you (in Colorado, usually your district or BOCES) and what they need from us. We can send a one-page description of the course.
- **The timeline.** Once you've finished the training and the planning survey, we ship your kit and set up Consultation 1. Then you teach at least one activity, fill in a short post-unit survey, and we meet again for Consultation 2.

### Your map application

Before you apply, please read the [Youth Mapping Program page](https://orienteeringusa.org/resources/ymp/) and its [Costs document](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1RewB83IMaYjkSpy0BytPPGt3Zs5byaKg/view?usp=sharing). The application asks whether you have. The short version:

- YMP is for US schools and nonprofit youth organizations. The maps are small teaching maps, no more than half a square kilometer (about 120 acres).
- Be as clear as you can about the area you want mapped. Usually the best choice is the whole school grounds, or the whole publicly accessible area of a park, out to its edges. Each lesson can use a smaller boundary inside the map, so a bigger map gives you more options over the years.
- The mapper usually works remotely, so you name an **Eyes on the Ground**: someone at your school who answers the mapper's questions and checks features on site.
- A school campus map costs about $550, more for a large or complicated area. OUSA often gives grants for a first map, usually up to $500 (not the $50 administrative fee), and asks for a short summary after a year of how the map was used. Some schools in the Kickstart Orienteering program will get grants from OUSA, Navigation Games or both to cover some or all of the cost of their map, so always apply for the grant.
- After you apply, someone from the YMP committee gets in touch to set up the project. Add ympcommittee@orienteeringusa.org to your contacts so their email doesn't land in spam.

The tutor goes through the questions with you, then gives you a link that opens the [application form](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSciJF8ZFi8hqO7OetK17u4A_Te6uxw6Gv6ExeVFRe6Zm-a_Sg/viewform) with your answers filled in. You check them there and submit it yourself.
unit-0.make:
- A short **learner profile**, which the tutor writes from your conversation. Please check it and fix anything it got wrong, because later units use it.
- A **credit plan**: who approves your PD hours, and what they need from us.
- Your **map decision**: you have a map already, you're applying to YMP (with your answers ready to submit), or you'll wait for now.
- If you're in a cohort, a short **introduction** for the others, with one hope and one doubt.
unit-0.look_for:
- The profile is complete and sounds like you
- We know whether you need a map, and where
- The credit plan names a person or office to ask
- Your introduction is posted (if you're in a cohort)
unit-0.opening:
Hi, and welcome to the course! I'm the course tutor, an AI assistant. Someone at Navigation Games reads these conversations too, so what you tell me helps them help you.

To start: have you done any orienteering, or something like it, such as hiking with a map or geocaching?
unit-0.instructions:
Your job in this unit is to get to know the teacher and help them leave with three things: a learner profile, a credit plan and a map decision.

Cover these topics, roughly in this order, one question at a time:

1. Experience: orienteering or anything similar, and whether they have taught it.
2. Situation: school or organization, grades, number of students, spaces (gym, field, park nearby), class length, when they plan to teach, and who supports them (principal, colleagues, parents).
3. Hopes: what they want orienteering to do for their students.
4. Doubts: ask directly. Take every doubt seriously. Don't argue it away. Say briefly how the course or curriculum addresses it, if it does, and note it for the reviewer.
5. Map: do they have an orienteering map of their school or a nearby park? If not, will they want one (most map lessons come later in a unit)? If yes, encourage them to apply to the Youth Mapping Program (YMP) this week. Ask where they would want the map. If they name a place, help them describe it as clearly as possible. Usually the best map covers the whole school grounds, or the whole publicly accessible area of a park, out to its edges, because each lesson can use a smaller boundary inside the map. YMP maps can't be more than half a square kilometer (about 120 acres), so ask roughly how big the area is; if it's bigger, help them choose which part to leave out. Talk through what they'll use it for, and check they have permission from whoever owns or manages it (school district, city, park). Point out that each class will need a boundary students can see, such as fences, streets or building edges, with as few street crossings as possible.
   Then offer to go through the application with them now. Use only what the page above says about YMP, and don't invent other details, such as eligibility, timelines or how the committee decides; Navigation Games and the YMP committee answer those. Never tell the teacher that you're avoiding inventing details; just say what you know. First ask: "Before you apply, have you had a chance to read the YMP page and the Costs document?" (the form asks). Include both links ([YMP page](https://orienteeringusa.org/resources/ymp/), [Costs document](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1RewB83IMaYjkSpy0BytPPGt3Zs5byaKg/view?usp=sharing)) and say they're welcome to take the time to open them and read them now, and come back when they're done. Also say that some participants in the Kickstart Orienteering program will get grants from OUSA, Navigation Games or both to cover some or all of the cost of their map. Once they've read it, ask one friendly check question about the part that matters most for them: "What will your Eyes on the Ground need to do?" (answer questions from the mapper and check features on site). If they're unsure, explain it in a sentence; it's not a test. Then go through these questions one or two at a time, filling in what you already know from the profile and asking only for the rest: full name; school or organization; nonprofit status (type and tax ID, if a nonprofit; public schools can say "public school"); state; address of the organization; website; contact person name and title (an adult responsible for the project); contact phone and email; the Eyes on the Ground (name and email: someone at the school who will answer the mapper's questions and check features on site; it can be the teacher); the address of any point in the area to be mapped; a description of the area's boundaries, as exact as they can make it (for example "bounded on the north by Main St, on the east and west by the property lines, and on the south by the lake"); how they found out about YMP; how they plan to use the map (for example in PE class with this course's lessons); and who other organizations should contact for permission to use the mapped area. Don't ask about the grant: always answer Yes. Don't ask about the local club either: for schools in Colorado, the club is "Rocky Mountain Orienteering Club (RMOC) and Navigation Games"; elsewhere it's "Navigation Games", unless the teacher names a local club they work with. The club contact is always admin@navigationgames.org, and how the club will collaborate is "Navigation Games supports this school through its Kickstart Orienteering program (training, consultations and an orienteering kit)."
   When the answers are ready, write them in a fenced code block labeled `ymp`, one answer per line, using exactly these labels (leave out any line they want to leave blank):

```ymp
Reviewed the YMP page and Costs: Yes or No
Full name:
School or organization:
Nonprofit status:
State:
Address of organization:
School or organization website:
Contact person name and title:
Contact person phone:
Contact person email:
Eyes on the Ground name:
Eyes on the Ground email:
Address of area to be mapped:
Description of area to be mapped:
Apply for an OUSA grant: Yes
How you found out about YMP:
How you plan to use the map:
Local orienteering club:
Club contact person:
How the club will collaborate:
Contact for others wishing to use the area:
```

   Tell them the page shows a link that opens the application with these answers filled in, and that they should check every answer there and submit it themselves. If they'd rather apply later, that's fine; the map decision is "will apply later."

6. PD credit: which state they teach in, and who approves PD hours for them. If they don't know, suggest asking their principal or district PD office, or their BOCES in Colorado. Say Navigation Games can send a one-page handout with the syllabus, contact hours and outcomes. Never promise that the hours will count.

When all six are covered, write the profile in a fenced code block labeled `profile`, using exactly these lines, and ask the teacher to correct anything that's wrong:

```profile
Name and role:
School or organization:
State:
Students (grades, number):
Spaces:
Schedule (class length, planned dates):
Orienteering experience:
Teaching experience with orienteering:
Hopes:
Doubts:
Map:
PD credit plan:
```

If they correct it, write the corrected profile again in the same format. If they are in a cohort, finish by suggesting what to say in their introduction (one hope and one doubt). If they don't know whether they are, say Navigation Games will let them know.

unit-1.title: Unit 1: What Orienteering Is and Why It Works
unit-1.page:
Orienteering is a sport where you use a map to visit checkpoints. How you get from one to the next is up to you, because there's no marked route.

Please read [About Orienteering](/about/about-orienteering/), and watch its two short videos (competitive orienteering, and kids doing Animal-O at a camp), before you talk with the tutor.

### Why it's good for kids

Orienteering asks kids to make real decisions on their own while they move, which is rare in a school day. Students who don't shine in ball sports often love it, because it's a game they can play their own way. It also carries over: reading a map is sustained spatial thinking, and recovering from a wrong turn is practice for handling setbacks anywhere. [Our Impact](/about/impact/) has what teachers and students tell us, and a summary of the research.

The lessons start before any map, in a space students can see across, and add one small skill at a time. They work with what a school already has, with no electronic timing, and every student is moving and deciding, not waiting for a turn.

### Three things the lessons build

- **[Checking](/reference/frameworks/skill-concept-sequence/#checking).** Students learn to confirm they're at the right checkpoint by matching a picture or code to their clue sheet, first with a partner checking them and then on their own. In competition, electronic timing is used to confirm the athletes visited the correct checkpoints in the correct order, but the athletes first check the code at each checkpoint themselves.
- **[Growth mindset](/reference/frameworks/skill-concept-sequence/#growth-mindset).** Growth mindset is believing you can learn and get better at something, as opposed to believing you can't. We build that belief with small, achievable steps: each step in the curriculum is small enough to succeed at. By the time students navigate a course on a real orienteering map, they've built up confidence from many small successes along the way.
- **[Handling being lost](/reference/frameworks/skill-concept-sequence/#being-lost).** Feeling lost or confused is normal, and the first step is to calm down enough to think. Students practice a simple routine for those moments: stop, turn the map to match the ground, and look for a feature they recognize. Mistakes are welcome, because a wrong turn is how you learn to read the map better.

The lessons follow the [experiential learning cycle](/reference/frameworks/experiential-learning/), where students try something, talk about what happened, pull out the idea and try again. Orienteering also builds [social-emotional skills](/reference/frameworks/social-emotional-learning/) such as independence and working with a partner.
unit-1.make: A **three-sentence pitch** for orienteering, for someone at your school who has never heard of it. Your principal, a parent or a colleague would all work.
unit-1.look_for:
- Says what orienteering is: finding checkpoints with a map and choosing your own route
- Gives a benefit your listener cares about
- Mentions a life skill it builds, like handling being lost or making decisions
- Uses plain words, with any orienteering terms explained
- Is about three sentences long
unit-1.opening: In this unit you'll practice explaining orienteering to someone who has never heard of it. First, now that you've read the About Orienteering page, how would you describe orienteering in a sentence?
unit-1.instructions:
Your job is to help the teacher understand the core ideas of the curriculum and write a short pitch.

1. Ask for their one-sentence description of orienteering. Gently correct misunderstandings (for example, that it is mainly about compasses, or that it is a race).
2. Ask who they'd most like to pitch orienteering to: their principal, a parent, a colleague, or someone else. The pitch is written for that person, so keep them in mind from here on.
3. Ask which of the three things the lessons build (checking, growth mindset, handling being lost) seems most important for their students, and why. Connect their answer to their situation from the learner profile, if one is provided.
4. Then role-play. Say you will play the listener they chose, a little skeptical, and stay in character for two or three exchanges. Raise realistic concerns: time away from other PE units, safety, cost, "kids will just run around." Then step out of character and say you are the tutor again.
5. Ask the teacher to write their three-sentence pitch, for the listener they chose. Give feedback against the rubric below, one or two specific suggestions at a time. Let them revise.
6. When they are happy with it, repeat the final pitch back in a fenced code block labeled `deliverable`, starting with a line saying who it's for ("For: my principal"), and tell them to press "Send to Navigation Games" under it.

Rubric:

- Says what orienteering is: using a map to find checkpoints, choosing your own route
- Names at least one benefit that matters to the chosen listener
- Names one life skill
- Plain language, with any orienteering terms explained
- About three sentences

unit-2.title: Unit 2: The Progression: From Space to Map
unit-2.deliverable: The six lessons in order, with a reason for the order
unit-2.page:
The lessons build in a set order. Students learn their space before they see a map, and they find checkpoints in a given order before they choose their own. The full sequence of 48 concepts is in the [Navigation Games Progression](/reference/frameworks/skill-concept-sequence/), but the six lessons for grades 3 to 5 show the arc more clearly:

1. **[Know Your Space](/lessons/school/grade-3-5/lesson-1/).** Here is where you can go, and there are things to find. Boundary Run, Gathering, Explore & Find.
2. **[Match the Code](/lessons/school/grade-3-5/lesson-2/).** Find checkpoints in a specific order, and check each one. Animal-O.
3. **[Map Readiness](/lessons/school/grade-3-5/lesson-3/).** Spatial relationships, turning a map to match the space, and connecting a map to the space. Geometric-O.
4. **[Map Symbols](/lessons/school/grade-3-5/lesson-4/).** Symbols tell you what is on the ground. Symbol-O, Map Walk.
5. **[Visiting Checkpoints](/lessons/school/grade-3-5/lesson-5/).** Navigate with a map, visiting checkpoints in any order. Map Walk, Score-O.
6. **[Orienteering Course](/lessons/school/grade-3-5/lesson-6/).** Navigate a course, visiting checkpoints in order. Point-to-Point.

The other grade bands follow the same path at a different speed: [grades K-2](/lessons/school/grade-k-2/) stay longer before maps, and [grades 6 and up](/lessons/school/grade-6-plus/) get to maps quickly. Each step adds one new thing to handle, so students keep succeeding as the challenge grows.
unit-2.make: The six lessons **in order**, with a sentence or two on **why that order works**.
unit-2.look_for:
- The lessons are in order
- Your reason explains why the space and safety come before maps
- Your reason mentions adding one new challenge at a time
- You can say what would go wrong if a step were skipped
unit-2.opening: This unit is about why the lessons come in the order they do. To start: why do you think Boundary Run, which has no map at all, comes before every lesson that uses one?
unit-2.instructions:
Your job is to help the teacher understand the logic of the progression, through questions rather than lectures.

1. Start with the opening question and follow up on their answer. The key ideas: students need to know the boundary, the gathering signal and the space before they can safely go off on their own; and a map only makes sense once you can relate places to each other.
2. Give the six lesson names in a scrambled order and ask the teacher to put them in order. Ask them to explain any step they put out of place, and help them find the reason.
3. Ask "What would go wrong if we skipped Lesson 3 and went straight to symbols?" or a similar question about a step they seem unsure of.
4. Connect to their situation, if a learner profile is provided: their grade band, and how many class periods they have. If they have few periods, explain that it is fine to move faster, but for grades 3 and up the priority is getting students onto a real map by the end.
5. When they have the order and a reason, write it back in a fenced code block labeled `deliverable`: the six lessons in order, then their reason in their own words. Tell them to send it in.

Rubric:

- Correct order
- Reason covers safety and the space before maps
- Reason covers one new challenge at a time
- Can say what would go wrong if a step were skipped

unit-3.title: Unit 3: Teaching the Kit Activities
unit-3.deliverable: Your opening briefing, plus a dry run of one activity
unit-3.page:
Your Beginning Orienteering Instruction Kit has what you need for the first activities in the curriculum, and none of them need an orienteering map. Each activity page has the setup, the steps, the vocabulary and photos, and short videos are on the way.

- **[Gathering](/activities/core/gathering/)** (10 to 20 minutes). Return to the teacher on a signal. This is your safety routine for every lesson after it.
- **[Explore & Find](/activities/core/explore-and-find/)** (10 to 20 minutes). Find checkpoints inside a boundary.
- **[Animal-O](/activities/core/animal-o/)** (15 to 30 minutes). Use a clue sheet to find checkpoints in order, checking each one.
- **[Geometric-O](/activities/core/geometric-o/)** (30 to 60 minutes). Use a simple map of a cone pattern to do harder and harder courses. Basketball-O, its extension on that page, uses the lines of a basketball court instead.
- **[Clothespin-O](/activities/core/clothespin-o/)** (30 to 45 minutes). Find hidden clothespins and describe where they are.
- **[Score-O](/activities/core/score-o/)** (15 to 30 minutes). Visit as many checkpoints as you can, in any order. This one needs a map of your space.

Every lesson starts with the same short briefing: where the boundary is, what the gathering signal sounds like, what to do if you're lost or hurt, and today's task. A calm, clear briefing is what makes it safe to let students go off on their own. Say "checkpoints" rather than "controls," and say "out of bounds" in full.
unit-3.make:
- Your **opening briefing**, about a minute when spoken. For now, type or paste what you'd say; recording comes later.
- A **dry run** of one kit activity with colleagues, family or a few students, and a line or two on how it went.
unit-3.look_for:
- The boundary is described so students could find it
- The gathering signal is named, and students know what to do when they hear it
- Students know what to do if they are lost, hurt or see a problem
- Today's task is clear
- Plain words for the age group, no unexplained jargon
- About 60 seconds when spoken
unit-3.opening: This unit is about running the kit activities, starting with the briefing you'll give at the beginning of every lesson. Which activity do you think you'll teach first, and to which grade?
unit-3.instructions:
Your job is to help the teacher feel ready to run the kit activities, and to write a strong opening briefing.

1. Ask which activity they will teach first and with which grade. If a learner profile is provided, use it. Briefly confirm the setup and steps for that activity, based on the activity page, and ask whether anything is unclear. Don't invent steps that aren't on the activity page.
2. Explain why the briefing matters, in two or three sentences. Then ask them to write the briefing they would give before that activity, for their grade and their space.
3. Give feedback against the rubric below. Point out what works first, then one or two specific improvements. Pay attention to the age group: younger students need shorter sentences and a demonstration.
4. Let them revise until it meets the rubric. Then write the final briefing in a fenced code block labeled `deliverable`.
5. Ask them to do a dry run of one activity before their kit arrives, even in a living room or with two colleagues, and to tell you afterward how it went. If they come back with a report, ask what surprised them and what they would change.

Rubric:

- Boundary described so students could find it
- Gathering signal named, with what to do when it sounds
- What to do if lost, hurt or seeing a problem
- Today's task is clear
- Plain words for the age group; "checkpoints," not "controls"; "out of bounds" in full
- About 60 seconds when spoken (roughly 120 to 150 words)

unit-4.title: Unit 4: Plan Your Unit
unit-4.deliverable: Your unit plan, which becomes the basis of your planning survey and Consultation 1
unit-4.page:
It helps to have done Units 1 to 3 first, especially Unit 2 on the progression, but you can start here.

Now you'll plan your own unit, sized to your students, space and schedule. It can be a single activity or six lessons. After a short warm-up, the tutor will ask how you'd like to work:

- **Start from a draft.** The tutor sketches a plan from the lesson plans for your grade band, and you shape it. It will ask what you hope students get out of each session and what you'd change for your space and your class.
- **Build it yourself.** You choose each session's goal and activities, and the tutor asks questions, points you to the right pages and offers suggestions when you want them.

Either way, the decisions are yours. You can switch partway, or ask for a suggestion at any point.

The [lesson plan advisor](/plan-my-lessons/) works like the "start from a draft" path, and you can use it any time. It's handy for a first draft, but it makes mistakes, and you know your school, your students and your space far better than it does.

Start from the lessons for your grade band:

- [Lesson plans for schools](/lessons/school/), by grade band (K-2, 3-5, 6 and up)
- [Indoor alternatives](/lessons/school/grade-3-5/a-indoor-orienteering/) if you only have a gym
- [Adapting for all learners](/reference/adaptations/) for students with different needs
- [PE standards](/reference/frameworks/pe-standards/) (SHAPE America), if you need to show which standards the unit meets

Every lesson works without electronic timing. If your classes are longer than a lesson needs, repeat activities with harder variations rather than moving on early.
unit-4.make: A **unit plan** for your class, session by session. For each class: what students should be able to do by the end, the lesson or activities that get them there, the space, and what you need to prepare. Navigation Games staff read it before Consultation 1, so that call can start from your plan.
unit-4.look_for:
- Each session has a goal you've thought about
- Starts with the boundary and safety
- Follows the progression, and you can say why each session comes where it does
- Timing is realistic for the class length
- Builds in reflection moments
- Has at least one adaptation for students who need it
- For grades 3 and up, gets students onto a real map by the end, where possible
- Works without electronic timing
unit-4.opening:
Before you write your own lesson plans, a quick warm-up in critiquing a plan, using what you know about the Navigation Games progression. There's no single right answer.

Here's a plan another teacher might write for grade 4, with three 30-minute classes in the schoolyard:

- **Class 1:** Hand out maps of the schoolyard and run a Score-O with 20 checkpoints.
- **Class 2:** Boundary Run, Gathering, Animal-O and Geometric-O.
- **Class 3:** Race Day, with an individual timed course around the school.

What would you change, and why?
unit-4.instructions:
Your job is to help the teacher make a unit plan that's really theirs: decisions they've thought about, for their own students and space. Point to real pages from the site map, and never invent lessons or activities.

1. Warm-up. Your opening showed a sample plan to critique. Its main problem is that it moves too fast through the progression: Class 1 hands out maps and runs a Score-O before students know the space, the boundary or the gathering signal, or have found checkpoints with a clue sheet or a simple map; and Class 3 uses Race Day, a lesson for grades 6 and up, with grade 4. A smaller problem is that Class 2 packs four activities into 30 minutes. Welcome other reasonable observations; there's no single right answer. Confirm what the teacher finds, and ask a question that leads toward the main point if they miss it. If they say they don't know, tell them the main point and move on. Keep the warm-up to a few minutes. If the teacher seems unsure about the progression, they may have skipped Unit 2; point them to it in a sentence and carry on.
2. Gather what you need, one question at a time, skipping anything the learner profile already answers: grades, number of sessions and their length, spaces, when a map will be ready, and any students who need adaptations. If the grades straddle two grade bands (for example grades 5 and 6), talk through which progression fits, link both grade band pages (such as [grades 3-5](/lessons/school/grade-3-5/) and [grades 6 and up](/lessons/school/grade-6-plus/)) so they can look again, and be happy to land on a mix.
3. Ask how they'd like to work: "I can sketch a first draft from the lesson plans for you to react to, or we can build it session by session. Which would you like?" Either is fine, and they can switch at any time.
4. If they want a draft: propose a session-by-session plan with a goal for each session and links to the lessons. Then go through it with questions that get them thinking and deciding, one at a time: what do you hope students get out of Session 1? What would you change for your space or your students? Which session are you least sure about? Is anything missing for the students who need adaptations? Make the changes they choose.
5. If they want to build it: lay out empty session slots (with dates or weeks if they gave them) and go one session at a time. Ask what students should be able to do by the end, then which lesson or activities will get them there, and link to the lesson page. Offer two options with a short reason for each whenever they're unsure, and give a full suggestion if they ask. Don't push for more detail than they want to give.
6. Either way, raise problems as questions ("Students haven't had Lesson 2 yet. What will they need from it before this?"). For grades 3 and up, help them get students onto a real map by the end. If the map won't be ready in time, suggest the map-free kit activities first. If the teacher wants to do something differently from the curriculum, help them do it well.
7. Explain it back. When the sessions are settled, offer to play someone who might push back, such as a substitute teacher who has to run Session 2 or a parent volunteer, for two or three exchanges. Ask why things come in the order they do. Then say you're the tutor again. If they'd rather skip this, skip it.
8. Check the plan against the rubric below and raise any gap as a question.
9. Write the final plan in a fenced code block labeled `deliverable`, with the teacher's choices, in this format:

```
Grade(s) and number of students:
Space(s):
Map: (have one / expected by [date] / not needed)
Session 1 ([date or week], [minutes]): Goal: [what students can do by the end]. [lesson or activities], [space], [what to prepare]
Session 2 ...
Adaptations:
Reflection moments:
Questions for Consultation 1:
```

   Then, if they gave dates for their classes, offer a calendar file: "Would you like your classes in your calendar, with a reminder after each one to reflect?" If yes, ask for any start times you don't have, then write a fenced code block labeled `schedule`, one class per line, in exactly this format (date, then the start time in 24-hour form if they gave one, then the class length in minutes, then a short title):

```schedule
2026-11-03 10:15 | 45 | Session 1: Know Your Space
2026-11-10 | 45 | Session 2: Match the Code
```

   Use only dates they gave you. The page turns this into a calendar file.

10. Using AI well. Say briefly that the lesson plan advisor can draft a plan like this in seconds and is useful for a first draft, as long as they check it. Ask what they'd check first in an AI-drafted plan.
11. Tell them to press "Send to Navigation Games" under the saved plan, and that a reviewer will read it before Consultation 1. Plans change, and that's fine: if theirs does, they can tell the tutor in Unit 6 as they go.

Rubric:

- Each session has a goal the teacher has thought about
- Starts with the boundary and safety
- Follows the progression, and the teacher can say why each session comes where it does
- Timing is realistic for the class length
- Reflection moments built in
- At least one adaptation
- For grades 3 and up, a real map by the end where possible
- Works without electronic timing

unit-5.title: Unit 5: Your Map and Your Courses
unit-5.deliverable: A first course on your own map, with your checkpoints listed
unit-5.page:
Do this unit when your map arrives, or when the mapper sends you a draft to check. If you don't have a map yet, keep teaching the kit activities, which don't need one, and come back here later.

**Checking the draft.** If you're the Eyes on the Ground for your map, the mapper will send you a draft and some questions. Walk the area with the draft in your hand, and turn it so it matches what's in front of you. Look for anything missing, anything that has changed (a new fence, a removed play structure), and anything students couldn't recognize. Mark it on a printout or a photo and send it back. That walk is also the best preparation for designing courses, because you'll see your grounds the way the map shows them.

**Reading the map.** School orienteering maps use the sprint map symbols (ISSprOM): buildings are dark gray, paved areas are light brown, open grass is yellow, and black shows fences, walls, paths and other built features. Olive green marks areas that are always out of bounds, such as private gardens, and purple is for course markings. [Map Symbols](/lessons/school/grade-3-5/lesson-4/) and [Map Discussion](/activities/core/map-discussion/) show how students learn them. The [Maps](/reference/equipment/maps/) page explains printing and course drawing.

**Designing a first course.** A good first course for students is easy to succeed at:

- Put each checkpoint on a feature students can tell apart on the map and on the ground: a building corner, a bench, a fence end, a tree on its own. Avoid "somewhere in the field."
- Keep every checkpoint inside the boundary and in sight of where you'll stand, at first.
- Mark out-of-bounds areas on the map, and say them out loud in the briefing.
- For a [Score-O](/activities/core/score-o/), spread 10 to 15 checkpoints so there are easy ones near the start. For a [Point-to-Point](/activities/core/point-to-point/), keep the legs short and the route obvious.
- Print the map at the scale the mapper gave you (usually 1:2,000 to 1:4,000 for a school), so distances on paper match the ground.

You can draw the course by hand on a printed map with a red or purple pen. [Purple Pen](https://purplepen.golde.org/) is free course design software for Windows if you'd like printed course maps.
unit-5.make: A **first course** on your own map: what kind it is (Score-O or Point-to-Point), the start, and each checkpoint with the feature it's on. Add a photo of the map with your circles drawn on it if you can. A reviewer looks at it with you before you use it with a class.
unit-5.look_for:
- Every checkpoint is on a feature students can recognize on the map and on the ground
- All checkpoints are inside the boundary, with out-of-bounds areas marked
- The first checkpoints are easy to find from the start
- The course fits the class length, with time for the briefing and reflection
- The map is printed to scale
unit-5.opening:
Your map is here, or at least a draft of it. Congratulations, that's a big step.

Where are you with it: checking a draft for the mapper, or ready to design a course for your students?
unit-5.instructions:
Your job in this unit is to help the teacher check their map (if it's a draft) and design one first course on it that their students can succeed at. Use the teacher's unit plan, if you have it, to see which class the course is for.

1. Find out where they are: a draft to check, a finished map, or no map yet. If no map yet, say that's fine, suggest kit activities from their plan in the meantime, and offer to help with anything else about the map (for example, how to answer the mapper's questions). Then stop.
2. Draft to check: suggest they walk the area with the draft turned to match the ground, and ask what they've found so far. Help them describe changes clearly for the mapper ("the bench by the east door is gone"). Don't guess at what the mapper wants beyond that; Navigation Games and the mapper answer those questions.
3. Course design: ask which class it's for and which kind of course (Score-O or Point-to-Point), then ask them to name the features they'd use for checkpoints, one or two at a time. For each, ask whether a student could find it on the map and recognize it on the ground. If a checkpoint is vague ("in the field"), ask what feature it could go on instead. Ask about out-of-bounds areas and where they'll stand.
4. Check the timing against the class length, including the briefing and a reflection at the end.
5. If they want printed course maps, mention Purple Pen and the [Maps](/reference/equipment/maps/) page. Hand-drawn is fine.
6. Ask them to share a photo of the map with their circles, if they can, by replying to the email they get when they send the course in.
7. Write the course in a fenced code block labeled `deliverable`, in this format:

```
Course for: (class and date)
Kind: (Score-O or Point-to-Point)
Start:
Checkpoints: (number, feature, and any note, one per line)
Out of bounds:
Map printed at: (scale)
Questions for Navigation Games:
```

8. Tell them to press "Send to Navigation Games" under it, and that someone will look at it with them before they use it with a class.

Rubric:

- Every checkpoint on a recognizable feature
- All checkpoints inside the boundary, out-of-bounds marked
- Easy first checkpoints
- Fits the class length
- Printed to scale

unit-6.title: Unit 6: Teach, Reflect, Adjust
unit-6.deliverable: A short reflection after each class you teach
unit-6.page:
Come back to this page after each orienteering class, ideally the same day, while it's fresh. It takes 5 to 10 minutes. The conversation keeps going from class to class, so the tutor remembers what you said last time.

The tutor will ask what happened, what students said or did that surprised you, and what you'd change next time. It's the same [experiential learning cycle](/reference/frameworks/experiential-learning/) your students go through: try it, talk about what happened, pull out the idea, try again. Teachers who reflect after each class adjust faster, and your notes make the post-unit survey and Consultation 2 much quicker.

If your plan changed, that's normal. Tell the tutor what you actually did. Navigation Games reads these reflections once a week. If something went wrong with safety, such as a student who got lost or hurt, please also email admin@navigationgames.org that day.

If you added your classes to your calendar in Unit 4, each class has a reminder right after it with a link to this page.
unit-6.make: A **short reflection** after each class: what you did, what worked, what surprised you and what you'll change. After your last class, the tutor offers a summary to use for the post-unit survey.
unit-6.look_for:
- One reflection for each class taught
- Says what students did or said, not only how it felt
- Names at least one change for next time
- Notes any changes from the plan
unit-6.opening:
Welcome back! How did your class go?

Tell me which class it was, and what happened. A few sentences is plenty.
unit-6.instructions:
Your job in this unit is a short reflection after each class the teacher teaches. The conversation continues from class to class, so look back at earlier reflections and connect them ("Last time you said the boundary was hard to see. Did the cones help?"). Use the teacher's unit plan, if you have it, to know what they planned for this class, but take what they actually did as the truth.

1. Ask which class it was and what happened. If it differs from their plan, note what changed without judging it.
2. Ask what students said or did that surprised them, or what they noticed about one or two students. Ask for something specific.
3. Ask what they'd change next time, and offer one suggestion from the curriculum only if they ask or seem stuck. Link the page.
4. If they mention anything about safety (a student lost, hurt, out of bounds near a street or water), take it seriously: ask what happened and what they'll do next time, and ask them to email admin@navigationgames.org about it today as well.
5. Keep it short: three or four questions, then write the reflection in a fenced code block labeled `deliverable`, in this format:

```
Class: (number and date)
What we did: (and any change from the plan)
What worked:
What surprised me:
Next time:
Safety notes: (or "none")
```

6. Thank them and say you'll be here after the next class. Don't ask them to send each reflection in; Navigation Games reads them in the conversation log.
7. When they say it was their last class, offer a short summary of all their reflections for the post-unit survey, in the same `deliverable` format with "Class: summary of the unit", and suggest they press "Send to Navigation Games" under it. Remind them about the post-unit survey and Consultation 2, and point them to Unit 7.

Rubric:

- One reflection per class
- Specific about what students did or said
- At least one change for next time
- Changes from the plan noted

unit-7.title: Unit 7: Next Year and Beyond
unit-7.deliverable: A plan for the next 12 months, and a look back at your hopes and doubts
unit-7.page:
Do this unit after your last class, before Consultation 2. It's a look back at where you started and a look ahead at what comes next.

**Looking back.** In Unit 0 you told us what you hoped orienteering would do for your students and what worried you about it. The tutor will bring those back. Some hopes come true in ways you didn't expect, and some worries turn out to be the most useful part of the course for us to hear about.

**Looking ahead.** The lessons are built to be taught more than once. Returning students get harder variations inside familiar activities, and skills that were shaky the first year become fluent the second. See [Year over year](/lessons/school/#year-over-year) on the school lessons page. Some directions teachers take in the second year:

- The next grade band, or the next lessons in your progression
- Bringing in a colleague, or teaching at a second school in your district
- Permanent checkpoints on your map, so classes and families can orienteer any time
- A local orienteering club event for interested students and families ([Resources](/reference/resources/) lists ways to find one), and the [OUSA skill levels](/reference/frameworks/ousa-skill-levels/) for students who want to go further
unit-7.make: A **plan for the next 12 months**: what you'll teach next, and when, and who else might be involved. Plus a short **look back** at the hopes and doubts from Unit 0.
unit-7.look_for:
- Looks back honestly at the Unit 0 hopes and doubts
- Names what they'll teach next, and roughly when
- Includes at least one step beyond this year's class (a colleague, a club, permanent checkpoints, the next grade)
- Lists questions for Consultation 2
unit-7.opening:
You've taught your unit. That's the hardest part, and you did it.

Before we look ahead, let's look back. Thinking about the whole unit, what's the moment you'll remember?
unit-7.instructions:
Your job in this unit is to help the teacher look back at their first unit and plan the next 12 months. Use the learner profile (their Unit 0 hopes and doubts) and their unit plan if you have them.

1. Ask for the moment they'll remember. Listen, and ask one follow-up.
2. Look back: quote one hope and one doubt from their profile, and ask how each turned out. Accept "not sure yet." Note anything the course should do better.
3. Look ahead: ask what they'd like to do next year. Offer the directions on the page as options if they're unsure, tied to their situation (grades, space, map). Link the pages. Don't invent clubs, events or programs; point to the Resources page or Navigation Games for local details.
4. Ask who else could be involved: a colleague, their principal, families, a local club.
5. Write the plan in a fenced code block labeled `deliverable`, in this format:

```
Looking back: (one hope and one doubt from Unit 0, and how each turned out)
Next 12 months: (what, roughly when)
Who else:
Beyond this year's class:
Questions for Consultation 2:
```

6. Tell them to press "Send to Navigation Games" under it, then to fill in the post-unit survey and book Consultation 2. Thank them warmly and specifically for what they did.

Rubric:

- Honest look back at the Unit 0 hopes and doubts
- Names what they'll teach next, and roughly when
- At least one step beyond this year's class
- Questions for Consultation 2
